item.title: California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures
item.description:
California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed seven bills on Monday that aim to increase transparency around data centers’ electricity and water consumption.

🔍 Overview

  • Data centers are expanding across the U.S., prompting protests over potential strain on power grids and local water supplies.
  • The new California legislation seeks to give communities better data and more say on how data centers impact electricity bills and water supply.

🧩 Legislative Details

Bill Requirement
SB 886, SB 1168, AB 2383 Direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup grid‑connection costs
AB 1577 Requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption
AB 2619, AB 2469 Require water‑use disclosures; AB 2469 also makes operators cover infrastructure‑upgrade costs
SB 887 Removes categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act, ensuring data centers undergo environmental review

⚙️ Why it matters

  • Without clear data, scientists have found it “extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
  • The disclosure rules begin next year but still won’t provide a full picture of consumption.
  • Two possible outcomes are outlined: (1) ballooning electricity demand could lead to costly new infrastructure that may be overbuilt if AI demand falls, passing costs to other consumers; (2) spreading fixed grid‑maintenance costs across more customers could lower electricity rates, but this depends on data centers contributing to distribution‑system costs rather than only connecting to high‑voltage transmission.
  • Water‑use data remain opaque; water providers have refused to share usage figures, and current disclosures only apply when seeking permits or business licenses, leaving year‑to‑year usage unclear.

📊 Perspectives

  • “I’m happy [AB 1577] passed,” Specht said, noting the difficulty in researching state offers.
  • “I wouldn’t say definitively that data centers have increased the cost [of electricity],” he added, acknowledging the lack of numbers to demonstrate either increase or potential savings.
  • As data centers’ power needs grow, monitoring their energy and water consumption becomes increasingly important.

#California #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #WaterUse

Source: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that

item.title: Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland
item.description:
Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland

Google has announced a €13 billion ($15.1 billion) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, marking the company’s largest single investment in the EU to date. This initiative includes a massive deal to purchase nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

⚙️ Key details

Scheduled for disbursement in 2027 and 2028, the investment will support Google’s map, search, and chatbot services through the following projects:

  • Data centers
  • Electrical grid improvement
  • Clean energy and battery projects

Google is expanding its existing site in Hamina and opening data center operations in three new municipalities:

Location Action
Hamina Expanding site on a “remarkable level”
Kajaani Opening data center operations
Muhos Opening data center operations
Vaala Opening data center operations

💡 Why it matters

Economic and Employment Impact Google claims the investment will create 37,000 jobs (7,000 permanent and the remainder during construction) and contribute approximately €3.6 billion to Finland’s GDP.

Energy Infrastructure To manage energy needs, Google has entered a purchase agreement for 50% of the energy output from one of Finland’s two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years. Regarding this “bring your own power” (BYOP) strategy, Ruth Porat, Google President and Chief Investment Officer, noted, “This is Google’s first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States.”

Operational Continuity Plant operator Fortum stated that this deal allows the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant to continue operating until its licenses end in 2050; otherwise, the plant—which provides about 10% of Finland’s electricity—would not have been able to operate past 2030. Following the news, Fortum shares rose 15.5% to their highest level in over four years.

Energy Demand Network operator Fingrid forecasts a 40% jump in energy consumption over coming years due to Finland’s data center boom.

#Google #Finland #AIInfrastructure #NuclearEnergy #DataCenters

Source: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
